To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the enzymes responsible for the production and degradation of the eCB 2-AG, DAGLα and MAGL, are present on the postsynaptic membrane in all layers of the human cortex, (2) the postsynaptic localization of DAGLα is regulated by synaptic activity, and (3) the presynaptic localization of MAGL, which is involved in the inactivation of eCBs, is regulated by the level of eCBs.

1) in the hippocampus, 2-AG is synthesized and degraded at the postsynaptic site of glutamatergic synapses and 2-AG signaling is modulated by presynaptic CB receptors, 3) in the neocortex and hippocampus, 4) the presynaptic CB1 receptor is localized to the perisomatic region of parvalbumin (PV)-positive interneurons, 5) in the neotectum,
1) The molecular machinery responsible for 3D-AG synthesis and degradation is present on both pre- and postsynaptic sites in the human neocortex.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of molecular components of eCB signaling and their functional role in the neocortex.
the molecular diversity of eCB signaling in different cortical layers, with special emphasis on the role of the eNOS-NO-cGMP signaling in the regulation of eCB-mediated plasticity.
the elucidation of the synaptic localization and functional roles of enzymes responsible for eCB metabolism, as well as with the identification of novel eCB receptors in the neocortex.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the eCB system plays a key role in the modulation of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic transmission in the human neocortex.

our results provide the first evidence that the molecular machinery responsible for the synthesis, degradation and inactivation of 2-AG is present at both pre- and postsynaptic sites in the human hippocampal formation, and that the distribution of the components of the machinery is not uniform, but rather is complementary, with pre- and postsympatic components localized in different layers and subfields.
the molecular composition of eCB signaling at excitatory synapses in the human cortex is very similar to that described in other brain regions, e. g. hippocampus, but with some differences.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have demonstrated that the molecular machinery for the synthesis and inactivation is present in the postsynaptic compartment of pyramidal cells and that the enzymes involved in 2-AG synthesis and degradation have different subcellular localizations.
the molecular composition of eCB signaling at synapses is highly diverse, both across different brain regions and within the neocortex.
the molecular machinery for eCB signaling in the human neocortex is very similar to that of the mouse hippocampus.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the endocannabinoids and their enzymes are present in a complementary manner at cortical synapses.
the molecular machinery for eCB signaling is highly compartmentalized and organized in the postsynaptic compartment in the neocortex.

the endocannabinoids and the endocannabinergic system are not only involved in the modulation of synaptic plasticity, but are also crucially involved in the development and maintenance of neuronal circuits. (2011).
